title: Gated instruction lifecycle sketch
body:
Context: quick personal sketch exploring the idea of 'instruction-level gates' — lightweight handles that let the platform (and customers) control whether particular instructions or instruction blocks are allowed, rate-limited, cached, or downgraded based on policy.

Why this feels interesting right now
- Customers asking for finer control: canary safety for risky instruction templates, per-instruction cost SLOs, and selective caching.
- Fits our routing + fallback story: we already have model variant fallbacks; extend to instruction gating means we can degrade semantics before switching models.
- Could reduce cost by dynamically narrowing fidelity for known-OK instruction patterns.

Rough feature idea (high level)
- Instruction is first-class: SDK/REST accepts an 'instruction_id' + payload. Customers can register instruction templates in Console or via API.
- Gate policy: per-instruction policy (allow/deny/bypass/soft-deny) + quality tier + cost budget + telemetry hooks.
- Runtime enforcement: serving runtime consults policy (local cached policy store) and applies transforms: e.g., compress, strip optional context, route to lower-fidelity model, or reject.
- Fallback flow: if gated action fails soft-deny, provide structured fallback (explain why + reduced response) to app.

User stories (scratchy)
- As an AI product manager, I want to mark a few prompts as 'experimental' so we can A/B them in prod without exposing full fidelity to all traffic.
- As an SRE, I want to throttle specific instruction types during peak load to protect latency SLOs.
- As a security officer, I want to deny instructions that invoke external tool-calls unless they pass approval.

API surface (brain dump)
- POST /instructions -> register template (name, schema, metadata, default_policy_id)
- GET /instructions/{id} -> view
- PATCH /instructions/{id}/policy -> attach/override policy
- request payloads can include instruction_id override (opt-in)
- admission metadata: policy_evaluation_id returned in response headers for traceability

Console UX ideas
- Instruction registry listing with usage, errors, hit-rate, cost-per-call
- Quick-toggle policies (allow, soft-deny, deny, throttle) with expected cost savings preview
- Rollout: canary % by route, by token bucket, or by user cohort

Runtime considerations / implementation rough notes
- Policy cache: consistent yet eventually consistent; prefer cached local store with TTL and change feed via control plane (similar to feature flags).
- Enforcement points: pre-tokenization (fast checks) vs post-tokenization (may need content analysis). Aim to do lightweight checks early to preserve latency.
- Interplay with KV cache: if instruction gating compresses context, storing the compressed KV cache needs separate keying. Decide whether compressed/low-fidelity KV is shareable.
- Impact on batching: gating decisions may fragment batches; try to co-locate same-policy requests for efficiency. Add policy-id to batching key.

Metrics & telemetry
- per-instruction: calls, avg latency, p95, cost tokens, fallback-rate, deny-rate, cache-hit-rate
- policy-eval latency distribution (how long policy lookup adds to request path)
- 'regression' signal: evaluate quality delta for gated vs full-fidelity across labeled eval set

Acceptance criteria (MVP)
- instruction registry + policy CRUD in API
- runtime consults policy cache and can soft-deny (respond with 200 + structured fallback) or transparently route to lowered fidelity model
- Console shows usage and fallback-rate for registered instructions
- Telemetry pipeline emits per-instruction metrics to Looker/Observability

Open questions / TODOs
- Q: ownership: product-hosted-api or serving-runtime? (need cross-team RFC)
- Q: policy language: config DSL vs simple toggles? Start simple toggles for MVP
- Q: security: how to prevent instruction_id spoofing? Signatures? Tenant-scoped registry.
- TODO: sketch API wireframes + console mockups (Ravi)
- TODO: add small eval harness (Maya) to measure quality delta for compressed instructions
- TODO: spike perf impact of adding policy-id to batch key (SRE/infra)

Related notes/links:
- Related feature: 'session-presets' (see users/session-presets-personalization-sketch.json) — overlap but instruction-centric rather than session-centric.
- Prior infra PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1983 (policy cache plumbing idea)

Quick risks
- Too many instruction ids => console/organizational overhead
- Fragmentation of batching = cost increase if not coalesced
- Users may expect immediate policy updates; TTL/consistency trade-offs matter

Next steps (personal plan)
- Draft RFC skeleton (1 pager) summarizing user problems + minimal API + runtime sketch (due in 1 week)
- Sync with Ravi (console) and Maya (eval) to align metrics
- Run internal spike: simulate 1000 instruction ids and measure batch fragmentation (SRE spike)

Notes to self: keep this lightweight. Aim MVP that is easy to understand by customers (toggle + % rollout) and easy for SRE to reason about (batch key strategy).

-- end of sketch --
